1.pericope_label: When the morning was come, all the chief priests and elders of the people took counsel against Jesus to put him to death: And when they had bound him, they led him away, and delivered him to Pontius Pilate the governor.

schools.summary: Robertson takes the morning meeting for a formal session held after dawn to ratify what had been done illegally in the night, and recalls that he was bound in the garden and before Annas and may have been unbound before Caiaphas. Ellicott finds no pretence in it but a rule, that sentence was not to be given at the sitting which heard the trial, and sees behind the whole scene a contest of jurisdictions, the ecclesiastical power seeking to make the imperial its tool and the imperial trying not to be used. Barnes alone gives the session business to do, since blasphemy was no offence at Roman law and a civil charge had to be found; he also says they dared not stone him as they afterwards stoned Stephen, for fear of the people, and supposes the binding no more than a tying of the hands. Lightfoot simply counts the breaches of their own canons.

Gill offers three reasons for binding him again: security, reproach, and that the Roman judge should take him at sight for a malefactor. Calvin grants the form of the morning session and denies the motive, holding that they kept the shape of judicial proceeding so as not to be suspected of haste; and he answers Barnes's argument about Stephen directly, since that stoning was a tumult and proves nothing about what was permitted, adding that had they been free to take life they would in their fury have murdered him themselves, whereas it was fitting that the Son of God be solemnly condemned by an earthly judge, that he might efface our condemnation in heaven.

Clarke holds that proceeding against a life by night was contrary to all forms of law, so that the separation and the daybreak reassembly were got up for appearance. Wesley makes the timing a matter of doors, the council chamber in the temple never being opened at night.

Henry makes the delivery to Pilate a necessity, the power of capital punishment having been taken from the Jews about two years before, which he reads as the sceptre departing from Judah; and on the binding he turns the fact round, that we who were held in the cords of our sins are loosed by his bonds as we are healed by his stripes.

Chrysostom supplies a motive rather than a constraint for the appeal to Pilate, since a death in secret would have left the reputation standing. Cyril of Jerusalem reads the journey as prophecy, the man bound and led away being the present carried to the king; when it is objected that Pilate was no king he answers from the Gospel that Pilate sent him to Herod, and notices that the same day made Pilate and Herod friends who had been at enmity, so that the first peace made by the peacemaker was between the men who condemned him.
Origen will not let the fact of the binding pass without remark, that they bound Jesus who looses them that are bound.

Augustine attends only to the order of the telling, the evangelist having brought the night down to morning, turned back for Peter's denial, and returned to the morning to go on. Jerome puts the morning session down to zeal rather than law, the chief priests watching the whole night with a view to a murder, and reports the binding as ordinary practice, the condemned being sent bound to the judge.

debates.question: Why did the council reconvene at daybreak?

positions.position: To ratify formally what had been done illegally in the night
To give the appearance of legality, night proceedings being contrary to all forms of law
Because their own rule forbade sentence at the sitting that heard the trial
To avoid the suspicion of haste, keeping the shape of judicial proceeding
Because the council chamber in the temple was never opened at night
To find a civil charge that a Roman governor could act on

outliers.claim: Reads the binding and leading away as the fulfilment of a prophecy about a present carried to a king, resolving the objection that Pilate was no king by the sending to Herod, and finding the first peace of the peacemaker in the reconciliation of the two men who condemned him.

Denies that the Jews lacked the power of execution, treating the stoning of Stephen as a tumult that proves nothing, and holds that the referral to Pilate was fitting rather than forced, so that the Son of God might be solemnly condemned by an earthly judge.

themes: When the morning was come, all the chief priests and elders of the people took counsel against Jesus to put him to death:
And when they had bound him, they led him away, and delivered him to Pontius Pilate the governor.

3.pericope_label: Then Judas, which had betrayed him, when he saw that he was condemned, repented himself, and brought again the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders, Saying, I have sinned in that I have betrayed the innocent blood. And they said, What is that to us? see thou to that. And he cast down the pieces of silver in the temple, and departed, and went and hanged himself. And the chief priests took the silver pieces, and said, It is not lawful for to put them into the treasury, because it is the price of blood. And they took counsel, and bought with them the potter’s field, to bury strangers in. Wherefore that field was called, The field of blood, unto this day. Then was fulfilled that which was spoken by Jeremy the prophet, saying, And they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of him that was valued, whom they of the children of Israel did value; And gave them for the potter’s field, as the Lord appointed me.

schools.summary: Robertson glosses the word rendered repented as being sorry afterwards, a word carrying no evil sense in itself since Paul uses it of his own regret, what was missing being the change of life that took Peter back to Christ. Barnes puts the contrast sharpest, true repentance leading the sinner to the Saviour where this led away from the Saviour to the gallows, and supposes Judas looked for a miracle of deliverance. Ellicott notices what is absent, that here there were no tears as there had been in Peter's, finds the Greek exact in the word for hanging, the same used of Ahithophel, and offers three explanations of the attribution problem. Lightfoot refuses the hanging outright and will not let the account in Acts be harmonised away, holding that the devil who had lodged in him three days caught him up, strangled him and flung him down; and on the prophecy he will have no error at all, since Matthew wrote Jeremy and his countrymen understood it, the rabbis putting Jeremiah first in the order of the prophets.

Calvin says Judas was not reformed but made uneasy, God opening the eyes of the reprobate far enough to feel their misery, and observes that principals gain nothing by distinguishing themselves from their agents, the crime of one man acquitting nobody involved in it. Gill sets out exactly what Jeremiah does and does not contain, and puts the casting down of the money in the paved chamber where the council sat.

Clarke turns the whole episode into evidence, since had Christ been condemned on a disciple's word the charge of imposture would have stood, whereas the same disciple recanted, declared his Master innocent, flung back the bribe and died. On the prophecy he reports the Hebrew apocryphal Jeremiah that Jerome was shown and thinks the words were put there to prop up this quotation. Wesley is briefest on the priests: how easily could they digest innocent blood, and yet they had a conscience.

Chrysostom says the priests knew they had purchased a murder and were condemned by their own consciences. Cyril of Jerusalem presses their answer hardest, turning their words round: shall he who took and returned the price of murder see to it, and the murderers not see to it, and if the price is polluted how is the deed not polluted too?

Jerome asks why men who would not put the money in the treasury shed the blood at all, grants that the quotation comes from Zechariah, and refuses to make it a falsehood, the Evangelist's business being the staple of doctrine and not words and syllables. Augustine canvasses every solution: he rejects the copies reading only by the prophet, since the older ones name Jeremiah; he supposes the name rose in Matthew's memory and was left standing because the Spirit guiding that memory meant it to, which displays the consent of the prophets, who spoke by one Spirit so that each word belongs to all; and he notes that it is Jeremiah who buys a field and pays silver for it, so the reader is sent to compare the two.

debates.question: How is the prophecy named as Jeremiah’s to be accounted for?

positions.position: The quotation is from Zechariah and the discrepancy is immaterial, the Evangelist’s concern being doctrine and not words
The name stood by the Spirit’s intention, displaying the consent of the prophets and sending the reader to the field bought in Jeremiah
Matthew wrote Jeremy and was understood, the rabbis placing Jeremiah first in the order of the prophets
A copyist’s slip of a single letter between the abbreviated names
An apocryphal Hebrew Jeremiah containing the words, itself probably written to prop up the quotation
He was caught up and strangled by the devil and flung down, the account in Acts being taken literally
He hanged himself and the rope broke, the fall accounting for what Acts records
He hanged himself, the horrors in Acts arising from a trembling hand that could not tie the noose firm

outliers.claim: Rejects the hanging as a suicide altogether, holding that the devil who had lodged in Judas three days caught him into the air, strangled him and threw him down, and refuses the usual harmonisation with the account in Acts.
Turns the traitor’s remorse into an apologetic argument, that the one man positioned to destroy Christ’s character instead cleared it by recanting, returning the bribe and dying.

themes: Then Judas, which had betrayed him, when he saw that he was condemned, repented himself, and brought again the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders,
Saying, I have sinned in that I have betrayed the innocent blood. And they said, What is that to us? see thou to that.
And he cast down the pieces of silver in the temple, and departed, and went and hanged himself.
And the chief priests took the silver pieces, and said, It is not lawful for to put them into the treasury, because it is the price of blood.
And they took counsel, and bought with them the potter’s field, to bury strangers in.
Wherefore that field was called, The field of blood, unto this day.
Then was fulfilled that which was spoken by Jeremy the prophet, saying, And they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of him that was valued, whom they of the children of Israel did value;
And gave them for the potter’s field, as the Lord appointed me.

11.pericope_label: And Jesus stood before the governor: and the governor asked him, saying, Art thou the King of the Jews? And Jesus said unto him, Thou sayest. And when he was accused of the chief priests and elders, he answered nothing. Then said Pilate unto him, Hearest thou not how many things they witness against thee? And he answered him to never a word; insomuch that the governor marvelled greatly.

schools.summary: Barnes says they had condemned him for blasphemy, knew a Roman governor would disregard that, and substituted treason; he agrees that a kingship was owned and qualified, and thinks the governor astonished by the meekness rather than by the want of a defence. Robertson supplies the pressure on the other side, that Pilate could himself be accused to Caesar for disloyalty, rivals and pretenders being common across the empire. Ellicott makes this the marvel of the sermon of the trial, that at the outset of his ministry the prisoner claims with entire calm to be the one before whom all will give account, and judges that the explanation of the kingdom satisfied Pilate.

Calvin faces the objection that he was not wholly silent and answers that a defence was at hand and voluntarily withheld: he was silent that he might now be our advocate, and his silence opens our mouth. He adds that it is shocking that the Son of God should be dragged before a profane man and tried on a capital charge, but that he was pronounced guilty on earth so that we might not be condemned in heaven.

Clarke thinks no answer was needed, the accusations having refuted themselves, and reads the silence as magnanimity, which confounded the priests but affected Pilate, who had no interest in admiring it.

Henry notices the hypocrisy of a nation disaffected to Rome suddenly professing concern for Caesar's rights, traces the charge to their own error that the Christ must be a king who would break the Roman yoke, and turns the trial round: he was arraigned that we might be discharged, and stood in that judgment that we might stand in God's.

Chrysostom explains why the charge had to change, since the priests knew Pilate cared nothing for the matters of their Law and turned to a charge of state, as they would afterwards do with the apostles; and on the answer he holds that kingship was owned and at once qualified, the kingdom being not of this world, supported by the reason that cannot be gainsaid, that the servants of an earthly king would have fought.

Origen has Pilate speaking not in doubt but affirmatively, as he would afterwards write it over the cross, so that the reply turns his own words into a confession; he holds Pilate unworthy of an answer, a man with no settled opinion, and makes the governor's astonishment a wonder at endurance, since it seemed a miracle that a man at a criminal bar should be unafraid of the death all men think terrible.

Hilary distinguishes the two formulas, thou hast said to the high priest who knew the Law and its promise of a Christ, and thou sayest to Pilate who did not, because the salvation of the Gentiles hangs on that present confession. Jerome says the man who asked unwillingly got some answer while the chief priests were judged unworthy of a word, and adds that a defence might have persuaded the governor to release him and so deferred the benefit of the cross. Augustine is occupied with the seam, Matthew here returning from the digression about the traitor, and holds that it matters nothing to the truth in what order the evangelists relate events.

debates.question: Why did he answer Pilate but not the priests?

positions.position: Because the unwilling questioner deserved some answer while the priests deserved none, and because a defence might have got him released and deferred the cross
Because Pilate too was unworthy, having no settled opinion
Because a little had to be said so that total silence should not be read as obstinacy
Because no answer was needed, the accusations having refuted themselves
Because a defence was at hand and voluntarily withheld, that he might afterwards be our advocate

outliers.claim: Distinguishes the two forms of answer given to the high priest and to Pilate, and makes the difference turn on the hearer’s knowledge of the Law, the Gentile’s salvation hanging on the present confession.
Treats the calm claim to be the final judge, made at the outset of the ministry and in a discourse giving no prominence to the mission, as the most remarkable thing in the trial.

themes: And Jesus stood before the governor: and the governor asked him, saying, Art thou the King of the Jews? And Jesus said unto him, Thou sayest.
And when he was accused of the chief priests and elders, he answered nothing.
Then said Pilate unto him, Hearest thou not how many things they witness against thee?
And he answered him to never a word; insomuch that the governor marvelled greatly.

15.pericope_label: Now at that feast the governor was wont to release unto the people a prisoner, whom they would. And they had then a notable prisoner, called Barabbas. Therefore when they were gathered together, Pilate said unto them, Whom will ye that I release unto you? Barabbas, or Jesus which is called Christ? For he knew that for envy they had delivered him.

schools.summary: Ellicott weighs the evidence for the fuller form of the prisoner's name as considerable though not decisive, points out that the patronymic wants a personal name beside it, and adds that since Abba was a title of honour for a Rabbi, the cry Jesus the Rabbi's son found more favour than Jesus the Nazarene; he also names the real motive as fear of losing influence and power. Barnes thinks Pilate counted on the popularity of Jesus against an odious robber and supposes the question was put in both forms; he states the judge's plain duty and then the difficulty, that had Pilate done it the Scriptures could not have been fulfilled, leaving the tension standing. Robertson observes that the two men set side by side were a leader of revolt against Rome and a claimant to a spiritual kingdom, so that the governor unwittingly matched the antagonistic forces of all time, and notes that the envy was the leaders' and not the crowd's. Lightfoot shows how ordinary the name was among the rabbis, and recalls that at the siege of the city watchers on the towers warned of the Roman stones with a cry that was the robber's own name.
Gill says the envy was written in their faces and their whole conduct, which had nothing to do with Caesar or justice, and agrees that notable here means infamous.

Clarke reports a manuscript with a marginal note that the oldest copies read the choice as between two men of the same first name, and explains the usual omission by the scruple of Christian copyists; he draws the conclusion the others leave, that knowing the motive to be envy it was the judge's plain business to disperse the mob and release the prisoner, and remarks that malice springs from envy as often as from anger. Wesley says only that they envied him because the people magnified him.

Chrysostom reads the custom as Pilate's second attempt at a rescue, devised so that the Jews should not be left the shadow of an excuse, and notices that the transaction runs backwards, the prince petitioning the people where the people usually petition the prince, and so making them more violent.

Origen is colder about the custom, calling it the sort of favour conquerors show the subjected until the yoke is riveted, though he grants it had Jewish precedent; and he turns the exchange into a rule of the inner life, that every man who does evil has Barabbas loosed in him and Jesus bound.
Jerome cites the Gospel according to the Hebrews, where the prisoner's name is rendered son of their master.

debates.question: What was the prisoner’s full name?

positions.position: The oldest copies gave him the same first name as Jesus, later struck out by copyists unwilling to share the Redeemer’s name with a murderer
The evidence for that reading is considerable but not decisive, though the patronymic does want a personal name beside it

outliers.claim: States plainly that Pilate was bound to release the prisoner once he knew the motive was envy, and then that the Scriptures could not have been fulfilled had he done so, leaving the two statements standing together and finding providence in the fact that sentence came from a man satisfied of the innocence.

Turns the choice between the two prisoners into a rule of the inner life, so that whoever does evil has Barabbas loosed in him and Jesus bound, and whoever does good has Christ loosed and Barabbas bound.

themes: Now at that feast the governor was wont to release unto the people a prisoner, whom they would.
And they had then a notable prisoner, called Barabbas.
Therefore when they were gathered together, Pilate said unto them, Whom will ye that I release unto you? Barabbas, or Jesus which is called Christ?
For he knew that for envy they had delivered him.

19.pericope_label: When he was set down on the judgment seat, his wife sent unto him, saying, Have thou nothing to do with that just man: for I have suffered many things this day in a dream because of him. But the chief priests and elders persuaded the multitude that they should ask Barabbas, and destroy Jesus. The governor answered and said unto them, Whether of the twain will ye that I release unto you? They said, Barabbas. Pilate saith unto them, What shall I do then with Jesus which is called Christ? They all say unto him, Let him be crucified. And the governor said, Why, what evil hath he done? But they cried out the more, saying, Let him be crucified.

schools.summary: Barnes allows that the governor's wife may have been satisfied of the innocence by other means and that her sleeping mind worked on what her waking mind feared, dreams being treated as indications of the divine will by Romans and Greeks as well as Jews; he notes that the release lay with the people and not the rulers, records that the question was put three times, and calls Pilate weak and irresolute. Ellicott supplies what can be known of the woman, the relaxation under the Empire of the rule against wives in the provinces and the apocryphal name and proselyte status; he pictures the council mixing with the crowd and whispering, marks this verse as the first naming of the manner of death, and says the question attested the judge's conviction and his cowardice together. Lightfoot produces a rabbinic parallel for the very phrase, a king's mother sending word to have nothing to do with that Jew. Robertson observes that Sadducees and Pharisees, who agreed on little, saw the peril together, and is harshest on the governor, a feeble protest from a flickering conscience and a scene closer to a lynching than a trial.

Gill thinks the crowd was worked on not by public oratory but by servants sent among the people with two arguments, that the court had unanimously condemned a blasphemer and that if he went free the Romans would take away their place and nation; and he observes that of everything alleged not one criminal act had been proved. Calvin refuses to excuse the crowd and still insists on the distinction, that they were not of their own accord hostile but sold themselves to gratify the priests, so that the death was demanded by the voice of the people, not because he was generally hated but because most had enslaved their tongue to the conspiracy of a few; and he reports Pilate's last argument, an appeal not to pity but to shame.

Clarke states flatly that God had appeared to the woman, testifying the prisoner's innocence and warning what would follow if the blood were shed; he sets the two cries of the crowd side by side, the Son of David a few days since and a murderer preferred now, and draws a lesson against corrupt pastors. Wesley sees why the word crucify came so readily, crucifixion being precisely what Barabbas had deserved, and adds that in their malice they forgot what precedent they were handing a Roman governor, which within a few years turned dreadfully upon themselves.

debates.question: What was the dream, and what standing has it?

positions.position: A direct appearance of God to the woman, testifying the innocence and warning of consequences
A troubled sleep working on what she already feared, dreams being taken for indications of the divine will in that world

outliers.claim: Notes that in demanding crucifixion the crowd handed a Roman governor a precedent which within a few years turned dreadfully upon themselves.

Insists that the crowd were not of their own accord hostile but had sold their tongue to the conspiracy of a few, so that the popular demand proves the influence of the rulers rather than a general hatred.

themes: When he was set down on the judgment seat, his wife sent unto him, saying, Have thou nothing to do with that just man: for I have suffered many things this day in a dream because of him.
But the chief priests and elders persuaded the multitude that they should ask Barabbas, and destroy Jesus.
The governor answered and said unto them, Whether of the twain will ye that I release unto you? They said, Barabbas.
Pilate saith unto them, What shall I do then with Jesus which is called Christ? They all say unto him, Let him be crucified.
And the governor said, Why, what evil hath he done? But they cried out the more, saying, Let him be crucified.

24.pericope_label: When Pilate saw that he could prevail nothing, but that rather a tumult was made, he took water, and washed his hands before the multitude, saying, I am innocent of the blood of this just person: see ye to it. Then answered all the people, and said, His blood be on us, and on our children. Then released he Barabbas unto them: and when he had scourged Jesus, he delivered him to be crucified.

schools.summary: Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson all trace the hand-washing to the rite by which the elders of the city nearest an undiscovered murder disclaimed the blood, Robertson noting that the middle voice makes it a washing for himself with a slap at the crowd in it, and Ellicott supposing the motive mixed and quoting a poet of Pilate's own time on the nullity of such ablutions. Barnes answers the gesture with the argument that a magistrate is bound to free an innocent man, and with Clarke reads the later history of the nation as the literal fulfilment of the imprecation. Ellicott enters three cautions against that reading, and Robertson is blunter still, that Pilate's guilt was not washed off either, that at bottom the sins of all of us nailed Jesus to the cross, and that the words are no excuse for race hatred. Lightfoot supplies the Roman practice of beating those to be crucified before the judgment seat.

Calvin compares the governor to sailors who let a storm carry them out of their course and refuses the excuse of necessity; he draws from the imprecation a moral about men who will not take the trouble to distinguish right from wrong and are abandoned to a fury that ends in cursing themselves, and observes that God nevertheless reserved a remnant. He sets the scene at its widest, the sole Judge of the world placed at the bar of an earthly judge and set between two robbers as though he were their prince, until the spectacle is met by the argument that the punishment due to us was laid on him. Gill treats the released robber as an emblem of those for whom Christ suffered, loosed when he was bound and acquitted when he was condemned.

Clarke joins Barnes in the argument from the magistrate's duty, since Pilate had the armed force at his command and could have cleared himself before the emperor; and he reads the destruction of the city as the imprecation's fulfilment, noticing that crosses ran short for the men and room for the crosses. Wesley records only that the custom of washing was as much heathen as Jewish.

Henry puts the release of Barabbas as an inversion of a proverb, the common course of providence being that the wicked is a ransom for the righteous where here the upright is a ransom for the transgressors; and on the scourging he observes how little sense it made, since a man already sentenced had no need of rods, and turns it at the end, that he was chastised with whips that we might not be for ever chastised with scorpions.

debates.question: What does the imprecation mean for the generations after?

positions.position: It was literally fulfilled in the destruction of the city and the later history of the nation
Only a fraction of the people were present, some rulers dissented, and the son does not bear the father’s iniquity except as he consents to it
The guilt was shared by all the actors and by us, and the words are no excuse for race hatred
The lesson is against the rashness that ends in cursing oneself, God having reserved a remnant

outliers.claim: Refuses to let the imprecation be read as a warrant against later generations, holding that the guilt was shared by every actor in the scene and that at bottom the sins of all of us nailed Jesus to the cross.
Reads the release of Barabbas as the reversal of the proverb that the wicked is a ransom for the righteous, the upright here being a ransom for the transgressors.

themes: When Pilate saw that he could prevail nothing, but that rather a tumult was made, he took water, and washed his hands before the multitude, saying, I am innocent of the blood of this just person: see ye to it.
Then answered all the people, and said, His blood be on us, and on our children.
Then released he Barabbas unto them: and when he had scourged Jesus, he delivered him to be crucified.

27.pericope_label: Then the soldiers of the governor took Jesus into the common hall, and gathered unto him the whole band of soldiers. And they stripped him, and put on him a scarlet robe. And when they had platted a crown of thorns, they put it upon his head, and a reed in his right hand: and they bowed the knee before him, and mocked him, saying, Hail, King of the Jews! And they spit upon him, and took the reed, and smote him on the head. And after that they had mocked him, they took the robe off from him, and put his own raiment on him, and led him away to crucify him.

schools.summary: Barnes and Ellicott take the hall for the governor's own residence, Ellicott specifying the Tower of Antonia whose portico faced the Temple court; Barnes reckons the band at a tenth of a legion and cannot imagine Pilate lending a fresh robe for a mockery, and takes the other side against Clarke on the crown, the shrub having sharp points of hard wood easily pressed into the skin so that the mockery increased the pain. Ellicott identifies the garment as the military cloak worn by emperors in their character as generals and suggests a worn one of Pilate's or the one Herod had used. Robertson traces the scarlet dye to the clustered insect that yields it. Lightfoot recalls a rabbinic tale of an angel in Solomon's shape holding a reed and struck with a reed.
Gill will not decide what plant the crown was made of and thinks it hardly matters.

Clarke argues that the crown was an instrument of ridicule and not of torture, that the plant was probably acanthus rather than thorn in our sense, and complains that Christians have gone astray in magnifying the sufferings from this one circumstance, painters being the worst commentators of all; he ends with the moral he found in an older writer, that Christ in this condition preaches to the kings of the earth that their sceptres are only reeds. Wesley says the robe was old and tattered.

Chrysostom counts the indignities rather than interpreting them: not one member but the whole body was made an object of insolence, the head by the crown and the reed and the buffeting, the face by the spitting, the cheeks by the palms, the whole body by the stripes and the robe and the pretended worship, the hand by the reed given it for a sceptre. He asks what plea we can have for resenting an injury after this, and observes that the soldiers had not even the Jews' envy to plead.
Origen makes the reed the broken staff of Egypt on which men leaned before they believed, taken up now to be triumphed over by the wood of the cross.

Jerome reads every article of the costume, the scarlet for the bloody works of the Gentiles, the crown for the ancient curse taken away, the reed as the instrument with which the sacrilege was written down. Hilary makes the scarlet the blood of all the martyrs and finds in the thorns the sins of the Gentiles that once pierced him, the crown of victory being woven from the prick in them; the reed is the frailty of the Gentiles he takes into his hand, his head struck with it so that their weakness may rest on the Father. Remigius keeps closer to the surface, the scarlet being the Lord's flesh reddened by his own blood and the crown his bearing our sins in the likeness of sinful flesh. Augustine harmonises the scarlet and the purple two ways and alone turns the changed clothing into an argument against those who said his body was a shadow.

debates.question: Was the crown of thorns meant to hurt or only to ridicule?

positions.position: Ridicule only, like the reed and the bent knee, the plant being probably acanthus
Pain as well, the shrub having sharp points of hard wood easily pressed into the skin
The plant cannot be determined and it hardly matters

outliers.claim: Holds that Christians have gone astray in magnifying the sufferings from the crown of thorns, blames painters as the worst commentators of all, and reads the crown as an instrument of mockery rather than torture.
Reads the reed as the frailty of the Gentiles taken into Christ’s hand, and the blow on the head as the means by which that weakness comes to rest on the Father, who is his head.

themes: Then the soldiers of the governor took Jesus into the common hall, and gathered unto him the whole band of soldiers.
And they stripped him, and put on him a scarlet robe.
And when they had platted a crown of thorns, they put it upon his head, and a reed in his right hand: and they bowed the knee before him, and mocked him, saying, Hail, King of the Jews!
And they spit upon him, and took the reed, and smote him on the head.
And after that they had mocked him, they took the robe off from him, and put his own raiment on him, and led him away to crucify him.

32.pericope_label: And as they came out, they found a man of Cyrene, Simon by name: him they compelled to bear his cross. And when they were come unto a place called Golgotha, that is to say, a place of a skull, They gave him vinegar to drink mingled with gall: and when he had tasted thereof, he would not drink.

schools.summary: Ellicott alone asks why this man was seized, noting the Jewish settlement at Cyrene and that the other evangelist names him as father of two men later known in the Church, and infers that he may already have been suspected of discipleship. Robertson explains the verb as a Persian word for impressing a courier, denies that a jest on Simon was meant, and lists what had gone before, Gethsemane, the betrayal, a sleepless night and the scourging. Barnes dissolves the problem of the drink by vocabulary, vinegar being thin wine gone sour and the common drink of the soldiers, myrrh and gall alike meaning anything exceedingly bitter, and records that the draught was commonly given to deaden the pains of crucifixion. Lightfoot divides the two accounts differently, taking the one for the national custom and the other for what was actually done, and says the cup was prepared not by the women who out of compassion paid for such drinks but by the persecutors.

Calvin makes the impressment an argument from bodily failure, since the men usually crucified were robbers of great strength who could bear such a burden, and the weakness that could not showed plainly that it was a lamb being sacrificed; he notes that the punishment was so detestable a man thought himself polluted if he put a hand to the wood, and that the evangelists record the name, country and children of a man taken from the lowest dregs, as though God meant to ennoble him by his heralds. Gill describes what the bare word crucified covers, the cross laid flat and the body raised on it until it died.

Clarke thinks the cross was carried part of the way by Christ himself and that Simon was made to assist rather than take it entirely; he sets out at length the conjecture that the discrepancy over the drink is a translator's, an original Aramaic phrase for sweet wine with bitters having been read as vinegar and gall, and is not satisfied with any of the reconstructions; and he says someone appears to have offered the cup out of kindness.

Henry supposes the place the common execution ground and perhaps the charnel-house where skulls were laid, and finds the fitness of it, that Christ in destroying death triumphed over it on its own ground; on the drink he makes the finest distinction of all, that he tasted it and would not drink it, taking the bitterness into his mouth because he would let no bitter cup pass untasted while atoning for our tasting of forbidden fruit, but refusing the opiate because he meant to feel himself die.

debates.question: Was the drugged cup offered in mercy or in malice?

positions.position: In malice, prepared by the persecutors rather than by the women who paid for such drinks out of compassion
In kindness, someone appearing to have offered it out of compassion
Neither is stated; the draught was simply the customary one for deadening the pains of crucifixion

outliers.claim: Infers from the naming of Simon’s sons, later known in the Church, that he may already have been suspected of discipleship, and that this is why the crowd seized on him out of all those present.

Distinguishes the tasting from the drinking, holding that he took the bitterness into his mouth so that no bitter cup should pass untasted, while refusing the opiate because he meant to feel himself die.

themes: And as they came out, they found a man of Cyrene, Simon by name: him they compelled to bear his cross.
And when they were come unto a place called Golgotha, that is to say, a place of a skull,
They gave him vinegar to drink mingled with gall: and when he had tasted thereof, he would not drink.

35.pericope_label: And they crucified him, and parted his garments, casting lots: that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophet, They parted my garments among them, and upon my vesture did they cast lots. And sitting down they watched him there; And set up over his head his accusation written, THIS IS JESUS THE KING OF THE JEWS. Then were there two thieves crucified with him, one on the right hand, and another on the left.

schools.summary: Robertson sees the incongruity of rough men casting lots for clothes, a comedy at the foot of the tragedy of the ages. Barnes and Ellicott both face the four different forms the evangelists give of the title and settle it the same way, by the three languages, the inscription needing not have run identically in each; Barnes adds the irony that the middle cross was the one Barabbas should have filled. Ellicott and Robertson both think the two robbers belonged to Barabbas's band, since no trial of theirs is recorded. Lightfoot fills in the word robber from the records of the period, the bands that burnt the palaces at Jericho and the daggermen who killed in daylight in the city.

Gill supplies what the bare word crucified covers, the cross laid flat, the arms nailed, the feet fixed on a basis in the upright, the whole raised and left standing till the man died. Calvin keeps to the shame of the place between the robbers, not set apart from them, which might have marked a distinction, but raised in the middle as though he were their prince, the finishing stroke of disgrace, needed so that he might stand in our room.
Clarke describes the custom of the placard and recalls that the priests asked for the wording to be altered and were refused.

Chrysostom notices two things nobody else does, that he was lifted up in the open air and not under a roof so that the air itself might be purified and the earth cleansed by what fell from him, and that the stripping was a particular contempt, the garments of the condemned being divided only when a man was too poor to leave anything else, which they did not do for the robbers.
Origen sets the title beside the plate on the high priest's forehead inscribed Holiness to the Lord, the true High Priest carrying his title on the cross.

Augustine takes the horror as the point, since it belongs to living rightly not to fear what should not be feared and no death was more fearful than this; and he runs through the history of wood, the ark that carried the race through the flood, the rod that divided the sea, the wood cast into the bitter water, the rod that drew the stream from the rock and the staff that held up the hands by which Amalech was beaten, so that by these steps we come at last to the wood of the cross, where Adam recovered what he lost at a tree. The Gloss adds that the four arms answer to the four quarters of the earth. Jerome cannot get over the enormity of the title, that after buying false witnesses and raising a riot they could find nothing to put on the board except that he was King of the Jews; and he finds the guard useful in the end, since the vigilance of soldiers and priests made the resurrection harder to deny. Remigius takes the title as providence, so that the Jews might learn that killing him would not rid them of their King. Hilary sees the whole race called to the Passion and divided by it, believers on the right and unbelievers on the left. Leo reads the same figure as the separation to be made at the judgment, the instrument provided for a punishment being made by the Redeemer into a step towards glory.

debates.question: How are the four differing forms of the title to be reconciled?

positions.position: By the three languages, the inscription needing not to have run identically in each
The wording is less important than its providential effect, that the sovereignty was confirmed by the instrument of death

outliers.claim: Argues that the open-air crucifixion purified the air and that the blood cleansed the earth, and that the dividing of the garments was a mark of special contempt reserved for men too poor to leave anything else.

Makes the cross the term of a long history of saving wood running from the ark through the rod of Moses to the ark of the covenant, and argues that the most fearful of deaths was chosen precisely to teach that no death is to be dreaded.

themes: And they crucified him, and parted his garments, casting lots: that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophet, They parted my garments among them, and upon my vesture did they cast lots.
And sitting down they watched him there;
And set up over his head his accusation written, THIS IS JESUS THE KING OF THE JEWS.
Then were there two thieves crucified with him, one on the right hand, and another on the left.

39.pericope_label: And they that passed by reviled him, wagging their heads, And saying, Thou that destroyest the temple, and buildest it in three days, save thyself. If thou be the Son of God, come down from the cross. Likewise also the chief priests mocking him, with the scribes and elders, said, He saved others; himself he cannot save. If he be the King of Israel, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him. He trusted in God; let him deliver him now, if he will have him: for he said, I am the Son of God. The thieves also, which were crucified with him, cast the same in his teeth.

schools.summary: Barnes calls the second taunt cutting irony rather than concession and explains the silence, since the time for the atonement had come and the people would have been no better satisfied had he stepped down; on the robbers he offers both explanations without choosing. Ellicott makes the finer point that the mockers bear unconscious witness to the truth, and finds it barely conceivable that priests and scribes should recite the very words of a psalm and so fulfil the prophecy, explaining it by their not reading that psalm as Messianic and by sheer familiarity. Robertson notes that they added to the psalm a word it does not have, the impatient now, and reads the imperfect as inchoative, the sense being even the robbers.

Gill takes the second taunt less as admission than insinuation, the cures and raisings being illusions or done by the Devil's help. Calvin agrees with Augustine that the plural is a figure, and adds that the evangelists meant only to show him attacked on every hand, down to the class of dying criminals; on the third taunt he finds Satan's sharpest arrow, the argument that God does not love those he does not immediately assist, and answers that nothing is less reasonable than to limit God's love to a point of time.

Clarke sets the offence and the answer side by side: a high priest who would destroy the temple, a Saviour who cannot save himself and a crucified Son of God are the contradictions that give offence, while rightly read they are a high priest opening a heavenly sanctuary, a Saviour dying as the victim of salvation, and a Son of God confining his power within the bounds of the cross.

Chrysostom turns the taunt inside out, since he does not come down from the cross precisely because he is the Son of God, having come for no other purpose than to be crucified; and on the robbers he says both reviled at first and not afterwards, using the fact as proof against collusion, the penitent having been a real robber and a real enemy first. Pseudo-Chrysostom hears whose voice it is, the father of these children having said once before, if thou be the Son of God, cast thyself down.

Jerome answers the promise of belief by comparing the miracles, since rising from a tomb is the greater and they did not believe that either, and adds that the demons, already feeling their strength broken, put the words into men's mouths to get him off the wood; on the robbers he offers the same sequence as Chrysostom with a cause, the withdrawn sun and the shaken earth working the change, or else reads the pair as the two nations. Leo turns on the mockers with a question, what teacher had told them the true King of Israel would be one who refused to be crucified, since the prophets spoke of a face not hidden from spitting and of a Lord who reigned from the tree. Hilary alone declines to soften the reviling of both robbers, taking it as a sign that the cross was bound to offend everyone, the faithful included. Augustine calls the plural a figure of speech standing for the singular.

debates.question: How is the reviling by both robbers to be squared with the penitent thief?

positions.position: Both reviled at first and one was afterwards changed, which proves there was no collusion
Both reviled until the darkness and the earthquake worked the change in one of them
A figure of speech, the plural standing for the singular
Either explanation will serve
The plain sense is to be kept, as a sign that the cross was bound to offend everyone

outliers.claim: Refuses to soften the report that both robbers reviled him, taking it as evidence that the cross was bound to be an offence to all mankind, the faithful included.

Treats the third taunt as Satan’s sharpest weapon, the inference that God does not love those he does not immediately assist, and answers that nothing is less reasonable than to limit God’s love to a point of time.

themes: And they that passed by reviled him, wagging their heads,
And saying, Thou that destroyest the temple, and buildest it in three days, save thyself. If thou be the Son of God, come down from the cross.
Likewise also the chief priests mocking him, with the scribes and elders, said,
He saved others; himself he cannot save. If he be the King of Israel, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him.
He trusted in God; let him deliver him now, if he will have him: for he said, I am the Son of God.
The thieves also, which were crucified with him, cast the same in his teeth.

45.pericope_label: Now from the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land unto the ninth hour. And about the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani? that is to say, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? Some of them that stood there, when they heard that, said, This man calleth for Elias. And straightway one of them ran, and took a spunge, and filled it with vinegar, and put it on a reed, and gave him to drink. The rest said, Let be, let us see whether Elias will come to save him.

schools.summary: Barnes calls the language neither Hebrew nor Syriac but a mixture, probably what he ordinarily spoke, and builds his answer to the cry in layers: the bodily anguish, the permitted return of the tempter in what was called the power of darkness, the withholding of consolations that have carried martyrs cheerfully to the stake, and beneath all something deeper, a manifestation to his soul of God's hatred of sin, endured in our place. Lightfoot supplies a rabbinic parallel in which Esther uses the same ejaculation, and reads the hour as the one when the chain was slackened and the whole malice of hell let loose at a single stroke.
Gill notices what else was happening at the ninth hour, the slaying of the daily sacrifice.

Clarke meets the error Hilary reports head on and refuses the suggestion that the deity departed at that hour, since take deity away from any redeeming act and redemption is ruined; and comparing the quotation with the psalm he says that as the evangelists give it, the language is neither Hebrew nor Syriac.

Chrysostom answers the same objection from duration rather than extent, an eclipse being transient where this lasted three hours, and insists on the opposite geography, the wonder lying in its covering the whole earth as had happened only once before, in Egypt at the Passover. He asks why nobody was converted by it, since the hour was chosen at midday and it was the sign promised to the generation that demanded one, and answers that the age was sunk in sluggishness and nobody troubled to look for its cause. Pseudo-Chrysostom keeps to the outrage, the creation being unable to bear what was done to the Creator, so that the sun withdrew his beams rather than look on it.

Origen states the astronomical objection before answering it, that an eclipse falls when the moon passes beneath the sun and cannot happen at the Passover when the moon is full, and that no Greek or foreign observer recorded it; he refuses to take refuge in a simple suspension of the laws of nature and concludes that the darkness, like the torn veil and the earthquake, was local. He also reads the hours, Egypt having three days of darkness and Judaea three hours, the light returning at the ninth as a promise for Israel; and on the cry he rejects the answer that it was said out of humility, asking the reader to measure the glory he had against the shame he accepted, and warning against taking the words after the manner of men.

Hilary reports the use heretics made of the cry, that the Word was absorbed into the soul, or that an ordinary man was left to die when the divine support was withdrawn. Jerome notes that a clause in the middle of the verse is superfluous to the Hebrew, holds it impious to read the psalm of David or Esther when the evangelist has applied its clauses to the Saviour, and offers two explanations of the bystanders, Roman soldiers who caught only the first word or Jews pretending to hear an appeal to Elias so as to charge him with weakness.

debates.question: How is the darkness to be defended against the astronomical objection?

positions.position: It was local to Jerusalem or Judaea, like the torn veil and the earthquake
It covered the whole earth, and its three hours’ duration already distinguishes it from an eclipse

debates.question: What does the cry of dereliction mean?

positions.position: Not humility and not mere misery; it is measured by the glory laid aside against the shame accepted
Not the departure of the deity, which would ruin redemption
Bodily anguish, the tempter’s return and withheld consolation, and beneath these a manifestation of God’s hatred of sin endured in our place
The hour when the chain was slackened and the whole malice of hell let loose at a single stroke

outliers.claim: Concedes the astronomical impossibility of an eclipse at full moon and the silence of secular observers, and answers by confining the darkness to Jerusalem or Judaea rather than claiming a suspension of natural law.

Holds against Origen that the darkness covered the whole earth, and explains the absence of conversions by the sluggishness of the age and the brevity of a single wonder nobody troubled to investigate.

themes: Now from the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land unto the ninth hour.
And about the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani? that is to say, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?
Some of them that stood there, when they heard that, said, This man calleth for Elias.
And straightway one of them ran, and took a spunge, and filled it with vinegar, and put it on a reed, and gave him to drink.
The rest said, Let be, let us see whether Elias will come to save him.

50.pericope_label: Jesus, when he had cried again with a loud voice, yielded up the ghost. And, behold, the veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom; and the earth did quake, and the rocks rent; And the graves were opened; and many bodies of the saints which slept arose, And came out of the graves after his resurrection, and went into the holy city, and appeared unto many.

schools.summary: Lightfoot makes a physical objection the others miss, that the tearing of a hanging can hardly be laid to the earthquake, a shock breaking hard things rather than soft, so that the curtain was a separate miracle. Barnes agrees with Jerome's rule and thinks the risen lately dead, since saints of an older generation would not have been recognised. Ellicott states the difficulties of the passage without flinching, that it stands alone in the New Testament and has been called a myth or explained away as bodies exposed by the shock, and sets against all of it the bareness of the telling; he connects the episode with the apostle's language about a preaching to the spirits in prison, and departs from tradition by refusing to identify the risen with the patriarchs of an apocryphal gospel.
Clarke attributes the opened graves to the earthquake without hesitation, taking the opposite view from Lightfoot of what a tremor could do.

Henry makes the loud cry the evidence, since the voice is among the first things to fail in dying men while this man spoke at the last like one in full strength, which shows that the life was not taken from him but delivered up; he hears in it a shout of mastery over the powers he was spoiling and calls it a trumpet blown over the sacrifice, and notes that the hour was that of the evening sacrifice and the killing of the paschal lamb.

Origen supposes two veils, the outer rent so that mysteries hidden until the Lord's coming might now be published, the inner waiting for a later unveiling; and he takes the signs inward, the shaken earth being all flesh, the rent rocks the depths of the prophets opened, and the graves the bodies of souls dead to God, which become bodies of saints when grace raises them.

Hilary reads the veil as dispossession, the nation dispersed and its honour withdrawn along with the angel who guarded it, and is bolder on the rest: the earth quaked because unequal to contain such a body, the rocks were rent because the Word that pierces all strong things had gone through them, and the graves opened because the bands of death were loosed. Augustine attends to the seams, fixing the rending at the moment of death by the words and behold, reconciling the centurion's fear with his wonder, and offering two ways of harmonising the women who stood far off with those who stood near. Jerome lays down the rule the others follow, that the graves were opened at the death but nobody rose before the Lord, that he might keep the primacy of the resurrection. Leo turns the signs into exhortation, that the rocks of unbelieving minds should be rent and those shut up in the sepulchres of mortality burst their bonds, so that what we believe of the body may happen in the heart.

debates.question: Was the rending of the veil part of the earthquake?

positions.position: No; a shock breaks hard things rather than soft, so the curtain was a separate miracle
Yes; the graves and the rocks and the hangings all yielded to the tremor

debates.question: Who were the saints that rose?

positions.position: People lately dead, who could still be recognised in the city
The question is not answered; what matters is that none rose before the Lord himself

outliers.claim: Sets out the standard objections to the account of the risen saints, answers them from the bareness of the narrative, links the episode to the apostolic language about preaching to the spirits in prison, and rejects the traditional identification of the risen with the Old Testament patriarchs.
Argues on physical grounds that an earthquake could not have torn a curtain, since a shock breaks hard things sooner than soft, and so treats the rending of the veil as a distinct miracle.

themes: Jesus, when he had cried again with a loud voice, yielded up the ghost.
And, behold, the veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom; and the earth did quake, and the rocks rent;
And the graves were opened; and many bodies of the saints which slept arose,
And came out of the graves after his resurrection, and went into the holy city, and appeared unto many.

54.pericope_label: Now when the centurion, and they that were with him, watching Jesus, saw the earthquake, and those things that were done, they feared greatly, saying, Truly this was the Son of God. And many women were there beholding afar off, which followed Jesus from Galilee, ministering unto him: Among which was Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James and Joses, and the mother of Zebedee’s children.

schools.summary: Lightfoot takes the centurion's confession at full value, as meaning that this was indeed the Messiah, a title the Jews themselves gave by adoption and deputation, the officer having picked up the expectation by living among them; he supposes both the sentences reported by the two evangelists were spoken, and follows an earlier scholar in identifying Mary Magdalene with the sister of Lazarus, arguing that otherwise she was either absent or passed over in silence. Barnes takes the confession low, pointing out that the Greek is a son of a god, a form suited to a polytheist, and supposes the sayings came from different men or at different moments; on the women he thinks they were kept back by the soldiers rather than by choice, and that not one of those who followed him is recorded as unfaithful. Ellicott insists that the words be interpreted from the centurion's knowledge and not from Christian faith, so that what they carried to him was one God-like in righteousness and holiness and love, and treats the other evangelist's report as a softening of the same witness. Robertson gives the group of women its epitaph, last at the cross and first at the tomb, refuses to guess at their anguish, and rejects the identification of Magdalene with the sister of Lazarus and with the sinful woman of the earlier chapter.

Gill asks where Peter was, who had said he would never be offended, and answers that none was present but one, while many women of the weaker sex stood there, which rebuked at once the earlier boasting and the present cowardice; he reports the derivations of the surname from the town, from a trade and from the Hebrew for a tower. Calvin puts the women's presence as providence rather than praise, that when the disciples were scattered the Lord retained some of their company as witnesses, and notices that although the one disciple did not leave the cross, no mention is made of him here, the commendation falling on the women alone.

Clarke says in Roman usage the phrase would mean an eminent or divine person and nothing more, praises the women for showing more courage and attachment than the men who had promised to die with him, reports the identification of Magdalene with the sister of Lazarus while himself distinguishing four Marys in the Gospels, and explains the distance at which the women stood by the fact that malefactors were crucified naked.

debates.question: What did the centurion mean by Son of God?

positions.position: That this was indeed the Messiah, a title he had learned from living among the Jews
No more than a deified hero, the Greek being a son of a god and suited to a polytheist
One God-like in righteousness and holiness and love, the words being interpreted from his own knowledge

debates.question: Was Mary Magdalene the sister of Lazarus?

positions.position: Yes, since otherwise that sister was either absent from the crucifixion or passed over in silence
The opinion is reported but four distinct Marys are to be distinguished in the Gospels
No, and she is not the sinful woman of the earlier chapter either

outliers.claim: Explains the distance at which the women stood by the fact that those crucified were stripped naked, so that modesty kept them back rather than the soldiers.

Reads the women’s presence as providence rather than merit, the Lord retaining witnesses when the disciples were scattered, and notes that the disciple who did stay is passed over so that the commendation falls on the women alone.

themes: Now when the centurion, and they that were with him, watching Jesus, saw the earthquake, and those things that were done, they feared greatly, saying, Truly this was the Son of God.
And many women were there beholding afar off, which followed Jesus from Galilee, ministering unto him:
Among which was Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James and Joses, and the mother of Zebedee’s children.

57.pericope_label: When the even was come, there came a rich man of Arimathea, named Joseph, who also himself was Jesus’ disciple: He went to Pilate, and begged the body of Jesus. Then Pilate commanded the body to be delivered. And when Joseph had taken the body, he wrapped it in a clean linen cloth, And laid it in his own new tomb, which he had hewn out in the rock: and he rolled a great stone to the door of the sepulchre, and departed. And there was Mary Magdalene, and the other Mary, sitting over against the sepulchre.

schools.summary: Ellicott finds Pilate's ready compliance of a piece with his earlier behaviour, a lingering reverence that helps the friends rather than the foes of the sufferer. Lightfoot explains the alternative, that the law forbade leaving a body on the tree overnight and that those executed by the council were buried not with their fathers but in one of two appointed grounds, the disgrace being reckoned to make some atonement. Barnes repeats Jerome's list of safeguards and adds one of his own, that the untenanted tomb answers the suggestion of a revival by contact with a prophet's bones, and explains that the spices were folded into the wrappings for want of time to embalm properly.

Gill notes that the man went in boldly, unashamed of a crucified Christ. Calvin credits none of the arrangement to design, holding that the untouched sepulchre came about by secret providence rather than premeditation, to distinguish him from the rest of the race and mark his newness of life.

Clarke turns the precautions around, since had he been buried in the common ground of executed men no one would have sealed a stone or set a watch, so that the very precautions of his enemies furnished the evidence; and he draws a line through the prophecy of a grave with the rich, that while still the sacrifice he was numbered with transgressors, but the atonement once made he is no longer enrolled with them.

Henry makes the point about the money without letting it pass unqualified, since worldly wealth is to many an obstacle in religion's way and yet in some services an advantage, and adds that Christ has more secret disciples than we know of.
Chrysostom admires the courage rather than the standing, a man risking his life and taking on many enmities, daring not only to ask for the body but to bury it.

Jerome answers at once why the man's wealth is mentioned, not to boast a noble disciple but to explain how he could get the body at all, since poor and unknown men would not have dared approach Roman power; and he gives three safeguards against fraud, a new tomb lest it be said another body had risen, a tomb cut in rock lest the foundations be said to have been undermined, and a stone no one could roll back without the strength of many. Pseudo-Augustine reduces the same to two objections foreclosed, that they dug through the ground and that they carried him off while the guard slept. Remigius reads the cloth, grown out of the earth and brought to whiteness by great labour, as the body taken from earth and brought through the passion to the whiteness of immortality, and ends with the women who marked the place so that at a fit time they might do their office. Hilary makes Joseph a figure of the apostles and the linen the sheet let down from heaven, so that the Church is buried with Christ, the rock-hewn chamber being the hard breast of the Gentiles cut open by the labour of teaching.

debates.question: Why is the burial described in such detail?

positions.position: To foreclose the charges of substitution, undermining and theft
Because the enemies’ own precautions became the evidence for the resurrection
Because a secret providence, not human design, obtained an untouched tomb to mark his newness of life

outliers.claim: Observes that a burial in the common ground of executed men would have drawn neither seal nor guard, so that the precautions taken against the resurrection are precisely what established it.

Reads the burial allegorically, the linen as the sheet let down from heaven and the rock-hewn tomb as the hard breast of the Gentiles opened by the labour of teaching, with the stone shutting out any later author of divine knowledge.

themes: When the even was come, there came a rich man of Arimathea, named Joseph, who also himself was Jesus’ disciple:
He went to Pilate, and begged the body of Jesus. Then Pilate commanded the body to be delivered.
And when Joseph had taken the body, he wrapped it in a clean linen cloth,
And laid it in his own new tomb, which he had hewn out in the rock: and he rolled a great stone to the door of the sepulchre, and departed.
And there was Mary Magdalene, and the other Mary, sitting over against the sepulchre.

62.pericope_label: Now the next day, that followed the day of the preparation, the chief priests and Pharisees came together unto Pilate, Saying, Sir, we remember that that deceiver said, while he was yet alive, After three days I will rise again. Command therefore that the sepulchre be made sure until the third day, lest his disciples come by night, and steal him away, and say unto the people, He is risen from the dead: so the last error shall be worse than the first. Pilate said unto them, Ye have a watch: go your way, make it as sure as ye can. So they went, and made the sepulchre sure, sealing the stone, and setting a watch.

schools.summary: Barnes lists the circumstances by which the enemies furnished the proof themselves, takes the governor's reply as leaving them the band already appointed for the crucifixion, and alone asks how a stone was sealed, offering cords closed with wax under a signet. Ellicott draws a sharp inference, that the priests had stirred the people by taking the words about the temple literally and yet had understood the real meaning themselves, seeing further here than the disciples because sorrow confuses while suspicion sharpens; he reads the governor's reply as a command to take a guard. Robertson meets the objection that the rulers could not have known of the prediction by pointing out that it was made to them expressly, and hears in the reply a curt permission thrown to men the speaker despised.

Gill reads the reply as a permission to take a guard, since if they had one already there was no occasion to ask, and ends with an irony, that if the tomb lay beyond a sabbath day's journey they broke their own tradition to secure it. Calvin puts the whole matter shortest, that with Pilate's signet they shut their own mouths as surely as they shut the sepulchre.

Clarke separates the two measures, the guard to stop the disciples stealing the body and the seal to stop the guard being bribed, and sees the priests refuting themselves, since they had killed him for the words about the temple taken one way and now declare the other meaning. Wesley identifies the guard as the garrison in the tower.

Chrysostom states most fully how the precautions defeated themselves, since the sealing testifies that he had died and been buried and if the tomb was watched no fraud was possible, so that an empty tomb proves the resurrection; and he adds a detail the rest miss, that Pilate would not let the soldiers seal it alone but made the priests do it themselves. He also notices that the evangelists conceal none of the opprobrious language, which shows both the savagery of the accusers and the truthfulness of the men who wrote it down. Cyril of Jerusalem answers the charge of deceit itself, that the cross was no illusion and the death no mere show.

Hilary calls the sealing folly and unbelief, the tomb of one at whose word they had watched a dead man walk out of another. Remigius takes up the arithmetic of the three days and rejects the expedient of counting the three hours of darkness as a night, giving his own reckoning from the day of the crucifixion through the sabbath to the Lord's own day. Augustine leaves the counting alone and reads the number, the three days answering to the consent of the whole Trinity in the passion. Jerome remarks only that crucifying him had not been enough: they must guard the grave as well.

debates.question: Did Pilate give them a guard or tell them to take one?

positions.position: He told them to take one, since men who already had a guard would not have come to ask
He left them the band already appointed for the crucifixion, still at their service
The words are a curt permission thrown to men he despised

outliers.claim: Notices that Pilate refused to let the soldiers seal the tomb by themselves and made the priests do it, so that they could not afterwards accuse the guard, and treats the whole arrangement as an unintended proof of the resurrection.

Infers that the priests had privately understood the saying about the temple which they had publicly misrepresented, and sees further into it than the disciples did, because sorrow confuses while suspicion sharpens the intellect.

themes: Now the next day, that followed the day of the preparation, the chief priests and Pharisees came together unto Pilate,
Saying, Sir, we remember that that deceiver said, while he was yet alive, After three days I will rise again.

Command therefore that the sepulchre be made sure until the third day, lest his disciples come by night, and steal him away, and say unto the people, He is risen from the dead: so the last error shall be worse than the first.
Pilate said unto them, Ye have a watch: go your way, make it as sure as ye can.
So they went, and made the sepulchre sure, sealing the stone, and setting a watch.
